utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The position in relation to Judge Nosworthy is the same as yesterday and we will continue today in her absence on the same basis. Mr. Stamp, the remaining parts of the eighth motion for Lukic to amend the 65 ter list. Can you assist or can Mr. Hannis assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I could assist poorly, but I know we filed a response. SO I don't know if you want to add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the problem is that a decision may be necessary for witnesses today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I'm not aware of a filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We did file something last evening, Your Honour, and Mr. Oren will be taking the next witness, Mr. Pantic, and it does pertain to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that maybe no action will have been taken as yet because it was after hours when it was filed. Do you have a copy of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have a copy at the moment but I'm sure we could print one out here and hand it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you could do that perhaps it can be printed and I can see what the position is as we progress. Meanwhile, we shall continue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, during the course of the day (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Another thing I wanted to say: If that is not sufficient, I am here and my material is in Belgrade. Could you please postpone your decision until Tuesday? By then I will have brought you piles of material to read to support my material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So piles of materials on lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's very interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Furdulovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In a moment we will continue with cross-examination by the Prosecutor. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth in all your answers which you made at the beginning of your evidence, that applies to your evidence today. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate for the record as I proceed that yesterday the witness clarified that the person who they had taken a statement from, the driver, was Ursuljanovic. I think that was one of the last things he said, and I could just indicate that that statement taken by the working group is in evidence, P578.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that -- is that a statement -- yes. Ursuljanovic, yes. Thank you. Are all the statements not part of the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All the statements that we obtained are part of the record. (redacted), but I got confused because I thought he was saying Jovanovic, and later on I realised it was Ursuljanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated, sir, that you were at least involved in obtaining a statement from Protic in 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while the translation is going on, could I have P3134 [Realtime transcript read in error P1314"].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was head of the operative team at the meeting of the operative team members of the operative team were appointed who were to take Protic's statement. After his statement was taken, I was made aware of the content of the statement. Directly in 2002 I did not take a statement from Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could you look at the document that should come up before you if we can -- I'll ask could we show the first page briefly and the last page. Just to put you in a position to say whether or not you could identify. But in all of his statements and in all of his interviews, Mr. Protic did tell you that he had transported corpses to Batajnica and to Petrovo Selo, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, P1314 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, 3134. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 3134, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the first page there. Can you make it out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we have a look at the last page briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the statement that officials from the working group took on the 28th -- or 27th of August, 2002 from Mr. Protic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the first and last page. I do not see the content, but the members of the operative team are Lakcevic Dusan and Gvozden Gagic, that is correct. The minutes were taken by Aleksandar Kostic, who was an inspector in the sector for investigating war crimes. So these were the members who were appointed to do this job, to interview Mr. Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at page 3 of this document and it's on page 3 in both the English and the B/C/S copy. You see the second paragraph after the Roman numeral II. Could you read that aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There it is now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He gave me a telephone number (Belgrade line) and a certain -- and a certain person whose instructions I would follow will call me at that number."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does it say that the person will call him or he would call the person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what is written here, a certain person was supposed to call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, he's saying that -- sorry, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. If I take a more careful look, this a bit confusing. He gave me a certain telephone number (Belgrade line) to which I was to be called by a certain person whose instructions I was supposed to follow." That would mean that this person would call him or that he would call this person. It is written in an ambiguous way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. And if you look to the preceding paragraph. Am I -- can we understand him to be saying that General Petar Zekovic gave him the number, gave him that number, with instructions that the person on that number, using that number, would give him instructions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the first paragraph, I think nevertheless that this is ambiguous, that the second paragraph is ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. It's not quite clear whether or not he would call or the person would call him, but what he's saying here is that he got that number from General Zekovic and that he was to receive instructions by telephone contact with the person on that line. Is that a correct understanding of what he said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It says that he got this telephone number from General Zekovic and that contact would be established on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you also to have a look very quickly at page 4 in the English, B/C/S -- page 4 to 5 in both the English and -- and the B/C/S copy. Can you read the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I was accompanied by Ceda Sakic who lives in Pancevo and who is now retired. General Zekovic gave me the Belgrade telephone number in order to call him when I arrive in Pristina."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you continue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing more. I can't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you go to the next page, please. I'd like to just confirm the ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: "I received all instructions and the telephone from General Petar Zekovic in the office of Nenadic Dragic in Autokomerc in the street of Omladinska Brigada in new Belgrade. "Now General Zekovic doesn't recognise me and does not remember what he ordered me. "The liaison person told me to contact such-and-such a person, asked me whether I knew where Petrovo Selo was, how many bodies I had on the truck, he gave me instructions to enter Kosovska Mitrovica and load the rest of the corpses. Already in Pristina I received an order from the same person to go to Petrovo Selo after having loaded the corpses and to unload them there. "I also make the following statement: "The first transport --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall from reading those passages that Protic always maintained that he will receive instructions from someone on that Belgrade line as to where to collect and take the bodies to, but he did not tell you who that person was in 2002?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to his statements, and there were several of them made orally, he changed his story. Once, as a matter of fact, he mentioned the name of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness -- okay. Go on. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So he mentioned a name that he refuted later. He first said that that was his contact person. It is true that several times he mentioned that out in the field he would get further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that in the course -- and I'm about to move on from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I asked that much be read because this was a rough draft translation and I think we will be applying in due course to get a CLSS translation of this document for the Court. This I should also indicate while I'm on this document is the full version of an extract 6D196 [Realtime transcript read in error "CD 196" ], which had been introduced in evidence earlier when Mr. Protic was testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the course of investigating the -- this new story and the press release from the public prosecutor for Negotin, you interviewed, and I think you said that, a significant number of police officers, and the procedure was that you would send a note, a request for approval to Mr. Lukic and that he approved every one. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately at the very outset we went out and conducted interviews with over 30 persons, most of them policemen. At the very outset we received approval and consent from Lukic to conduct interviews starting with the chief of SUP of Bor and then with all the policemen who we believed had certain knowledge in respect of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was it a normal procedure in the police at that time that in the course of investigations you would seek the approval of the chief of the police, the chief of the RJB, in order to interview someone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we were not duty-bound by law to start the kind of activity that we did start. Our task in accordance with the decision made by the minister was to check the reliability of the information that was made public. However, we made a plan, an operative plan of our work, and then following the information that was published in Timocka Revija we thought that first we should go to the Bor, Negotin, and Kladovo areas and conduct interviews with all persons, police and civilians. That is to say that at that time that was not the usual procedure. However, we had General Lukic's oral approval, and we went out into the terrain and did this job immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So in other murder investigations, and you'd agree with me I'm sure that this was a murder investigation once, but you had discovered in other murder investigations you would not necessarily or it was not the norm to be seeking the consent of the head of the department before you interviewed persons that might have information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is always customary to ask for approval of one's immediate superior. Not a single policeman can make a statement unless his immediate superior is aware of that beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But not necessarily the chief of the RDB.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The standard practice would be to get the consent of the police officers' immediate superior but the standard practice would not be to get the approval of the chief of the RDB.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of SUP in Bor is the ranking officer there. Below him is the chief of the OUP of Kladovo. That is to say that in order to talk to policemen of the OUP of Kladovo where Tekija is, where the refrigerator truck was found, we had to seek approval first from the chief of SUP as the ranking police officer in the area. When we received approval to talk to him, then we automatically got a possibility to talk to the rest of them. That is to say that we had the approval of General Lukic to conduct these interviews with all these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But -- but you also, I think from those documents that you were shown yesterday by learned counsel Mr. Aleksic -- sorry, Mr. Ivetic, you -- I think you indicated that you sought his approval even to interview civilians in some investigations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Approval is never sought for civilians. According to the Law on Criminal Procedure and other laws that are in force in Serbia we have the authority to interview civilians according to Article 226 of the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Can we -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you think the question has been answered. I'm afraid I don't share that. As an example, can we have on the screen 6D1610. That's one of the documents you were referred to yesterday, and one of the witnesses you wished to speak to is flag bearer Jovic Rade. Now, why do you need the approval of the chief of the RDB to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the status was at that time of Rade Jovic, but I think that these are commanders of the 3rd Platoon of the 37th Company of the PJP. I don't know what platoon he commanded, but as far as I can remember he's a platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why do you need the approval of the chief of the RDB to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's a member of the ministry, then there has to be approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: From the man at the top. Not from his immediate superior. You say you have to get approval in all these cases from the man at the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all cases we had to get approval from the man at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if you want to interview a cleaner in the ministry, you have to get Mr. Lukic's approval.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our work plans, we did not use cleaners as sources of information. In the cases that we had, that we handled, all -- they all involved policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but what if a cleaner was a witness to a crime being committed in the premises. Are you saying that that person -- that before you could interview that cleaner you would have to have the approval of Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We always needed approval for all members of the RJB sector. We would get this approval from Mr. Lukic. Sometimes it would be in writing and sometimes it would be oral, but in every case we obtained an approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that would apply to any inquiry, not just this case, but any inquiry that was being made that involved interviewing members of the staff of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now only speaking about the members of the RJB sector. In cases at that we handled at the time, we always sought approval of the chief of the sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure about what -- what you just said. Are you saying in all criminal investigations you sought the approval of the chief of a sector, like the chief of the RDB sector, prior to interviewing witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the second time that instead of RJB we have RDB. I don't know how it's being translated into Serbian, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- if we could have that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The first mistake is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to raise at that point, Your Honour, but I think the witness understood at that time, but I understand -- I'm following the translation that's coming through the way it is in the transcript now, and for the record, I think I will have to -- well, I think Mr. Stamp's question misstates the testimony of the witness, but I can't go into further details without perhaps prompting the witness, so I'll just let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It only misstates it in respect of not confining the witnesses involved to those who are part of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to understand you, and I'm not quoting you now. Am I to understand you to be saying that in other investigations, not these that we were discussing in these documents, in all other criminal investigations that you know of you would seek the prior approval of the chief of the RJB sector before interviewing witnesses who were attached to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that. I said that my answer applied only to the RJB sector. All cases that we handled, the refrigerator trucks, Bitiqi case, Berisa, Berisa brothers case, were all the cases where policemen were members of the RJB and they were our source of information, and for that reason we sought consent of the chief of the RJB. The cases where policemen were not members of the RJB there was no need for us to seek consent of General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just check one thing before I move on. I think you have before you 6D1610. Can you just read item 4 for me. You will see close to the bottom of the page a list of names. Could you just read what item 4 says.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Warrant Officer First Class Jovic Rade." Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Yes, I just wanted to clarify the translation. Could we look at 6D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm now, I'm afraid, further confused. Can you give me an example of a policeman who is not a member of the RJB sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these documents all of them are members of the RJB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you've just given an answer that in English says: "The cases where policemen were not members of the RJB, there was no need for us to seek consent of General Lukic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, give me an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the cases that we handled, there was no such example. I can't remember one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me just a general example so I understand the distinction you're making.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a member of the ministry worked in the administration for combatting organised crime, we did not need to seek approval of General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the administration for combatting organised crime does not belong to the RJB sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In such a case who would -- who would you require to approach for approval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would seek approval from the minister or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could -- could we look at 6D1611, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These -- is it there yet? This is a document of March 2002 in which you're also seeking the approval of General Lukic to interview certain persons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is in respect of the bodies of the Bitiqi brothers that were found at Petrovo Selo; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read out item 6 for me, the name that is at item 6.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ljubomir Andric, janitor at the MUP training centre in Petrovo Selo."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he a member of the RJB, or was the janitor a civilian?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, I wish to clarify so that it's clear. In addition -- or, rather, next to the names there is a position that the person performed during that time. For example, if we say Ljubomir Andric, janitor at the training camp of MUP in Petrovo Selo that means that's the job he performed at the time. The approval was sought for all of these people because at the time when the approval was sought they were all members of the RJB sector. Ljubomir Aleksic number 1 was the deputy chief of the police administration of MUP for the Republic of Serbia and then all of them, all the rest of them were members as well. This is where this misunderstanding arises. Approval was sought from the chief of the RJB because at that particular moment when the approval was sought they were members or worked for the RJB. However, at the time when the event took place they performed other duties or worked elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So are you saying that Andric Ljubomir was not a civilian, the janitor was a policeman? Just a moment. I don't wish to make any comment that might appear adverse but I can hear counsel speaking in Serbian from here, and I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to try to clarify, Your Honour. I think that the translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are two issues, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- as the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can deal with that by asking the witness to read it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but there is another issue. I would just want to say to the Court that -- and I'm not saying that anything wrong but -- was said or done but counsel should not converse at all so that I can hear from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've dealt with this before, Mr. Stamp. I'm -- I can hear -- I did hear sound. I don't know the circumstances because I wasn't looking in that direction, but it often happens when earphones are being worn and people speak louder than they would normally because they forget that their hearing is dulled by the earphones. So everyone should be particularly conscious of trying to remember to remove these before conversing in court. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it was indicated that there might be difficulty with the translation. Can you re-read item 6?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ljubomir Andric, janitor at the MUP training centre in Petrovo Selo."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would rather translate it as a superintendent, not janitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask the interpreter again to listen carefully to what the witness says and see if that's appropriate or not. Could you please read that line again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Ljubomir Andric, janitor at the MUP training centre in Petrovo Selo."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in our opinion superintendent is an American term used in large US condos. That has the same meaning the word "janitor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's a matter for submission in due course but in any event it seems to me it doesn't matter. Even if he was a civilian, my understanding of the evidence at the moment is that authority would be sought because he was part of the staff of the RJB. Mr. Stamp does appear in his questions to see it somewhat differently, but the answers of the witness so far have conveyed to me the impression that it wouldn't matter how low or high the employee was and what status that employee held, authority would be sought from Mr. Lukic. However, don't be dissuaded from your line of examination by that comment, Mr. Stamp, if you feel it requires further investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And prior to -- before those names you see at item 3, Goran Radosavljevic, and at item 5 we see Radomir Djeric, who had responsibilities in the Gendarmerie. Was the place where the bodies were found at Petrovo Selo part of a training camp that the MUP Gendarmerie used, and isn't that why you sought to interview the janitor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pit where the bodies were found is outside of the compound of the training centre. I personally opened up that pit together with the -- with a prosecutor and a judge. We interviewed everyone we believed might have useful information. It was done in accordance with the plan and we made no exceptions as to who we would interview. We interviewed people regardless of their position, title, and we always sought approval to interview them. By your leave, we interviewed over 17 persons, and the case was tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. Protic testify in that case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive information to that effect, but I know that Mr. Protic gave a statement to an investigator of the OTP and that he also testified before the District Court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you -- in your evidence you said that the FBI were involved in the investigation of the Bitiqi brothers. Do you know if the US authorities charged anyone in respect to those -- sorry, I -- I withdraw the question. Did you seek to interview General Lukic having regard to the fact that he was the head of the MUP staff for Kosovo and most of the bodies were identified to be bodies of Kosovo Albanians? Did you seek to interview him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. We didn't seek to interview Mr. Lukic because we had no information indicating that he had anything to do with the war crimes or with these crimes that had been committed. Yesterday I mentioned that we handled a couple of these cases, that all of these cases were brought to trial and that we could not conduct any investigation in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija for the well-known reasons. I'm convinced that had we had any information linking Mr. Lukic to this, we would have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you saying that you only interviewed persons who you had information that they had something to do with war crimes, that is, the exclusive category of person that you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very outset we interviewed five assistant ministers, generals. I tried to ensure the presence of the former minister of the interior and also chief of the RJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But those ministers, those persons on these lists, these janitors, these members of the Gendarmerie, the people that you interviewed, they were interviewed, I take it, because they were linked by information you had to these war crimes. Is that the only reason why you interviewed them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are saying you didn't interview General Lukic because you had no information that he was linked to war crimes. I'm asking if that is the only condition, if that's the only reason why you interview someone, because you had information that the person was linked to war crimes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attempt to talk to the minister and the chief of RJB and the generals, all those efforts were made -- already made in order to get a general picture concerning the mass grave. If you remember the first task of the working group was to verify the veracity, accuracy, of information concerning the Timok region. So first we tried to talk to people who would lead us -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. I just wanted to ask you one simple thing. The only reason you interview somebody, I take it from what you've said, is whether or not they had information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question he if he says "from what you've said" when the witness is as we can see from the transcript trying to say something and Mr. Stamp is interrupting when he's talking precisely about this topic. If you look at page number 19, line number 8, he's explaining this topic and Mr. Stamp's cutting him off and then asking a question "based upon what you said," well, he can't ask that question if he won't let the witness say and finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer required of that question was yes or no, so I think Mr. Stamp was quite right in interviewing -- in interrupting because if he wants more information he can ask for it. But the question demands a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say to this question is as follows: In addition to formal interviews that have certain records, there is also operative work conducted by the police, and this doesn't necessarily mean that a person is involved in commission of a crime if this work is conducted by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I take it from that that you are saying that a person did not need to be involved in a crime for you to ask some questions. So I come back to this then: The -- let's take a look at paragraph 8 of your statement, and I'll get to this. You had news reports in respect to the Berisa family in The Guardian and the BBC. Do you know when these news reports were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the text of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When, when? I asked you when. Do you remember when they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know that at the very outset of our investigation on the 30th of May, we opened up the mass grave in Batajnica. We commenced our intelligence work at the time. Thirty-six bodies were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked you when. That's all I asked you, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that piece of information. I can't tell you that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You -- you discovered that there were the bodies of the Berisa family, an entire family, in that grave at Batajnica, and you discovered at the time, I take it, that this was a crime that was committed in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Lukic was the head of the MUP staff for Kosovo at that time? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, as an investigator, weren't you interested to find out how an entire family, a clan almost, three generations of one family -- or four generations of one family, could have been killed, wiped out, and transported to Serbia and it escaped the attention of the chief of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view the question is unintelligible. What we were interested in, we performed. We proved that the crime had been committed. We conducted all interviews, and the case was brought to trial. I am really not able to discuss somebody's role in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just asked one question. If at that time you did not think that General Lukic might have had information as to the circumstances -- or let me put it this way: Might have helpful information about the circumstances in Kosovo at the time. Didn't you think so? Yes or no? I mean, if you didn't, you didn't.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what we thought, because we had original information about the crime that was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you know at the time that that crime, the -- the killing of the Berisa family, was one of a list of crimes that was on the indictment charging Mr. Milosevic and others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you would not know, then, whether or not General Lukic or anybody asked your war crimes working group to investigate other crimes that were listed on the indictment against Mr. Milutinovic -- Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not deal with that issue because we were not equipped either in terms of personnel or in terms of equipment to deal with cases that were larger than the ones that we dealt with, and I left the service in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You left in 2003 or 2004?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of February, 2004, I was appointed to the position of the chief of internal control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. What I really asked you, though, is whether or not your having discovered the bodies of a family that the ICTY indictment claimed were murders in Kosovo. You were asked to investigate the other events that the indictment referred to, the other events of murder that the indictment referred to. Simply were you asked by General Lukic or anybody else to investigate those other claims in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- you will agree with me that the -- this case we're talking about, the Suva Reka case, the indictment in Serbia was issued on the 24th of April, 2006? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But when you had left these persons, these policemen, weren't indicted, were they, or nobody was indicted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which policemen you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you had left, no one had been indicted for the killing of the Berisa family, when you left your job in the war crimes section. Is that so? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, object on foundational grounds. There's been no showing of the bases how this individual in the position he was would know what the workings of the Ministry of Justice of Serbia are since he's not a member of the Ministry of Justice or involved in the Ministry of Justice 's work in preparing indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was one of the police officers in charge of investigating the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. You may answer the question. If you don't know the answer, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were there in that role, nobody was indicted for that crime in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that it's nobody, but I know that quite a few cases that we worked on had to do with prosecutions before the judiciary. For Bitiqi we sent an entire case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking about --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us, as for police work, well, I told you about the Berisas. Forty-four statements we sent to the prosecutor's office in charge. That is the moment when our work stopped. It is the prosecutor who is in charge of all the rest. When the prosecutor took over the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Furdulovic, you're being asked about the Suva Reka case as you now recognise and it's a prominent case in your country, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an ongoing trial at the moment, is there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard from a colleague, a policeman, that the trial was under way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the question Mr. Stamp is asking you is when you left your job in connection with the investigation of these crimes, is it the case that no proceedings had been taken against anyone? Do you know the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case no proceedings were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just give us a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry I have to clarify something from you. If you kindly go back to page 25, line 9 -- now, I would just repeat what you have said and the translators may kindly give the Serbian version of the same. You said and I quote in your answer: "In my view, the question is unintelligible. What we were interested in, we performed. We proved that a crime had been committed. We conducted all interviews and the case was brought to trial." Now, important thing is I quote: "I was really not able to discuss somebody's role in this." Did you know anybody's role in this, because you said that you had the original information and so you did not require any other documentation. Could you please throw more light on this after what you have said, because what I suspect, that you have information. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the information that we had available at the time and that we worked with at the time, we had information that a specific person had committed a particular murder. His nickname is Cegar, as far as I can remember now. This information along with all the rest was sent on to the prosecutor in charge. When I say I don't know whether someone was indicted, that is to say that I don't know whether at that time an investigation was opened against such-and-such a person, and I don't know whether an indictment was issued. However, at any rate, I knew -- I heard, rather, that there were proceedings under way against this person. So this is our initial information, and I think that that is now under way according to our information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You have mentioned about the perpetrator, according to yourself, but there you are talking of the roles which can be beyond somebody's actually doing something. So would you like to speak on that, on the roles of different people into this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say role, it means in addition to the direct perpetrator of the crime there are persons who are eyewitnesses to the incident and there are persons who have general information, that is to say who are neither eyewitnesses, accessories, accomplices or perpetrators but they do have information that could be of assistance in a police investigation. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But when we talk of a role, it means somebody's participation. It don't mean somebody witnessing. He doesn't have a role. He's just an onlooker. So there's a difference between an onlooker and a person with a role but what we understand in a criminal law is a person having a role is a participant. Have you anything to say on this, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I do distinguish between a role in the judiciary, namely whether somebody is an instigator, aider, abettor, perpetrator, and on the other hand role in terms of operative work. When I'm saying "role," I'm talking about everything that we did as policemen and the role that a particular person had during the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately how many bodies were disinterred cumulatively from Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and Perucica? Perucica which is lake Perucac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, while I was there about 700 bodies were exhumed in Batajnica. In Petrovo Selo, the pit that was opened there -- in both pits, rather, there were about 70 to 77 corpses. I cannot be more precise on that. In Perucac I think around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these were the bodies of Albanians that could be determined then, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in the identification or the autopsy. It was the judiciary organs that were in charge of that, so I really don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but as one of the chief investigators you would want to know whether the bodies were identified or if they were identified as coming from a clan or a group of people, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And at all meetings with international representatives, the OSCE, the fund for humanitarian law, I insisted that an autopsy and identification be carried out as soon as possible because we do have this information linking us up to a particular location and the movement of a unit, possibly an individual, a group in the area. So the very fact that personal ID is found next to the body doesn't mean anything in a police investigation. However, the autopsy in 2001 was very slow, very slow indeed. It was even interrupted at the end of 2001. So that is the basic reason why this case was worked on for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you have -- did anybody apart from Protic tell you about how the bodies were transported from Kosovo to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything for sure now, but I think that the key information regarding the transportation came from Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further. There is one clarification I think I should make to the transcript. I referred to the Exhibit P3134 and indicated that the Exhibit 6D196 was an extract thereof. I think that the transcript did not record it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It might have said CD, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: CD, yes. I offer that correction. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Furdulovic, just a few questions for you. First of all, since there appears to be some confusion still in this proceeding -- in these proceedings, under the system in place in Serbia at the time, and I believe even now, who initiates indictments?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what entity is the prosecutor's office affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can the police -- strike that. Does the prosecutor's office have a legal obligation to inform the police, even the investigating police, of the progress of any case file submitted to them by the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is dominus litus. He is in charge of the proceedings. He does not have the duty to give -- return information to the police. As a matter of fact, he can give instructions to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just waiting for the translation and transcript. I think we've got the full answer now. When the police -- in your specific case when you handed over files to the respective prosecutors' offices for the proceedings that we discussed here, could you tell us what was contained in the documents that you -- generally speaking, could you describe what was contained in the documents that -- that were presented? That is to say, apart from the facts that you collected, the raw facts that you collected, did you also submit any conclusions or recommendations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall right now but I know that all 44 statements were sent after 38 persons were interviewed. I think that we compiled a report on the basis of these statements. However, I cannot remember specifically now, but in practice in order to make a concrete report we have to sublimate all the most important information that we gathered during the police investigation. By your leave, we as the work group and later on the department or division we always compiled reports on our action with regard to a particular case. These reports are now in the dossiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time period when the working group was doing its work, at that time within the Ministry of Interior had the RDB been separated from the Ministry of Interior at that point in time or was it still part of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told that the translation is again having trouble with that acronym.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The RDB the state security sector, was it still part of the ministry of the interior at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RDB, the republican state security sector, got out of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the RDB was separated out from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN FURDULOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that completes my redirect examination. Thank you, Mr. Furdulovic, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Furdulovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you dealing with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's Mr. Momir Pantic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this ninth application -- sorry, is it eighth application relates to him, and we now have the response of the Prosecution. So it might be best if we were to take the break now and consider the position in relation to the application to amend the 65 ter list. So if we break now and resume at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The outstanding matters in the eighth motion for the accused Lukic to amend the 65 ter list fall into two categories, a group of documents to be dealt with through the Witness Pantic, that's 6D1534 to 6D160, and secondly, two documents to be dealt with through the witness Bogunovic, 6D1616 and 1617. In their response the Prosecution have not dealt with the last two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection only regards the documents through Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. In these circumstances, we will allow amendment of the 65 ter exhibit list to include 6D1616 and 1617. So far as the others to be tendered through Pantic are concerned we will not allow the list to be amended to include them, and that is because of the timing of the presentation of such a large volume of material, much of which is untranslated, which has given the Prosecution inadequate time to prepare to deal with the evidence of the witness, and therefore we refuse to allow 6D1534 to 6D1602 to be added to the exhibit list. We will also require the Pantic 92 ter statement to be redacted to reflect this decision. We are still working on the exact requirements that follow, but I will be able to intimate these to you in the course of the evidence of the witness. You can deal with his statement in the normal way, and we will defer a final decision on its admission until the situation in relation to redaction is clear. So we can now have the witness Pantic -- sorry, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this representation is not correct. In his statement, we have 27 documents of which all are translated but one. So all exhibits from 6D1534 until 6D1559 are translated, and only untranslated document is 6D1560, and only those documents are included in Pantic's statement. And the Prosecutor has these translated documents since the time we wanted to include it through Paponjak. All those documents were translated at that time as well. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to deal with that, Mr. Oren? The suggestion is that your response totally misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, our submission relates to the eighth motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Where all those documents are listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My understanding is that there are 69 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Yeah. In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not 37 -- or 27 is it, Mr. Lukic? Sixty-nine is my understanding. Now, which is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The motion includes 69, but Mr. Pantic's statement includes only 27. I wanted to exactly avoid this situation, so I included only translated documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The position is therefore that the Bench has not had a proper understanding of the situation. We shall need to skip this witness and move to another one if you want to lead this evidence, Mr. Lukic, because if you will continually present material at this stage in the case that you've been in for three years, then inevitably you're putting us under a pressure that we can't sustain and deliver proper decisions. So who is your witness after -- we will revoke the decision I've announced at the moment. We will reconsider the position as soon as we can. Which other witness can we deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other witness is scheduled for 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, that's hopeless as well. I've repeatedly said there should always be another witness available in case of the situation such as this developing. A witness can -- anything can happen to a witness at any time waiting to give evidence here. It's just not acceptable conduct of litigation of this nature to be tendering material at this stage in this form. We can only do -- it would be very tempting to say we will refuse everything, but of course that's not doing justice to you. We have to reflect on the accurate presentation of the material, and we obviously have not done that, so we will reconsider it, but we can't just snap our fingers and do that. We need time to do that, just like you constantly bleeped about pressure that's put on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to say, but regarding the witness -- having another witness at the same time, we have the instruction from the victims and witness unit not to have witnesses here at the same time for too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, for too long, but in this situation where you don't even know what position the Bench is going to take in relation to your documents, there should be some back-up. As it is, if that's the position, we shall go off and deliberate on your motion further in light of the additional information. We shall consider it further. We'll take our time. We'll use the time. That time will be charged to you because you have created this situation, and we will resume, if we can, at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In light of the misunderstanding about the extent to which the documents would be spoken to by the Witness Pantic under which we proceeded, we have reconsidered our decision on the outstanding parts of the Lukic eighth motion to amend the 65 ter exhibit list, and we have decided that where documents to be presented through Pantic have been translated, in view of the nature of these documents the Prosecution should be able to deal with them in spite of the late notification, and given -- and bearing in mind the witness's familiarity with the documents we should allow them to be added. However, we consider that it's too late to add other documents, a large number of which are untranslated, in respect of which no reason is given for the late intimation, and no indication is given of why it is necessary to add them to the list at this stage. We will therefore allow to be added to the list numbers 6D1534 to 1559. That means that the only one being referred to by Pantic which is not being added is 1560, which is untranslated. As a result, we will ignore the reference to that document at the end of paragraph 56 of the statement and will not require a redacted version of the statement to be uploaded. We will refuse to add items 1560 to 1602, and as we indicated earlier, we will also allow to be added items 1616 and 1617. I hope that that deals with everything now satisfactorily, and if you wish, we can proceed with the evidence of Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we would like to call Mr. Pantic as our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like -- I need help from usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you is a statement. Could you please take a look and tell us whether that is the statement that you gave to the Defence of Mr. Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you were to be asked the same questions today would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would move and ask Your Honours to admit this statement as Defence Exhibit number 6D1604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pantic. Now probably some of my colleagues from the Defence will have some questions for you and then the Prosecutor will ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March, 2006, did the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal conduct an interview with you in Belgrade, I think?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Was this interview attended by our colleague Jelena Nikolic, I believe, who is a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if her first name is Jelena, but she's a lawyer from Novi Sad if that's who you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that you mentioned then that from October 1999 for almost three years you were unemployed -- or, rather, that you were involved in court proceedings with the Ministry of the Interior because of your unlawful dismissal from the position that you held in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I was not unemployed. I was unsatisfied with the fact that I was assigned a different job. I was still an employee of the Ministry of the Interior, and I had a decision of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I wasn't very specific. Were you involved in court proceedings before a court in Belgrade because you were dismissed from a position that you had held until then? As far as I understood, you were head of the OUP of Istok in 1998 and 1999. That's my understanding of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right that on that occasion during that interview you stated that even before the war with NATO started you and not only you personally but the entire OUP of Istok, the entire staff there, that you had some misunderstandings and conflicts with the local leadership there? I'm primarily referring to the chief of district there and to the chairman of the SPS there and the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I did not have a personal conflict. We processed from a police point of view the said persons because of the humanitarian aid that was coming in from Serbia in 1998, and they abused that humanitarian aid. They mostly used it for their own personal needs rather than having it distributed to the population, because this aid was being sent from Serbia proper and from Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So that is why the police filed criminal reports against some of them, because of the suspicion that they had violated Article 242, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: The police did deal with this and brought this to a very end, however, politics stepped in. As far as I understood the matter, Mrs. Gorica Gajevic intervened and said that this should not be taken to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that sometime in the beginning of March 1999, precisely because they were not pleased with the fact that you were doing your job a letter was sent to the minister or the leadership of the administration of the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade? They complained not only of your work but also the work of the OUP of Istok in general if I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: They complained about the work of the Ministry of the Interior in Pec as well, because the processing of these persons was not only carried out by the police officials of the OUP Istok but there was an entire team that was set up by the Pec police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct that during that interview with the authorised representatives of the OTP you said that from the 28th of March of 1999 practically you were sidelined and that this decision was made in Belgrade at the headquarters of MUP there and that another man, another colleague, was sent from the Pec SUP who was practically the head of the OUP of Istok?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I said -- I didn't put it in those terms. I said that my conflict happened when the commander of the 69th Detachment appointed the president of the municipality as his deputy on the staff. The president of the municipality beforehand asked me for a police uniform. He asked me to put a police uniform on him. I refused to do that. After that he was given a military uniform so that the president of the municipality would be the deputy head of staff as well. He was a self-proclaimed commander. And then the president of the municipality was proclaimed deputy commander, and he abused that terribly. He asked me that I should ask on his -- act on his instructions and his orders, and I refused to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all contained in your statement. Now I would like to ask you to have a look at paragraph 53 of your statement, and you say there, I'm referring to the first sentence, you say: "An erroneous understanding of resubordination by the commander of the Territorial Detachment," and so on and so forth, "led to the fact following constant complaints against you. The commander of the 3rd Army adopted a certain document." In relation to that could we see in e-court P1720. I'm just interested in the very beginning, that is to say before this word "I hereby order the establishment of the commission." If you can read this, only the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: "On the basis of reports from citizens of Istok municipality --" I do apologise for reading so fast. "On the basis of reports or information from citizens of the Istok municipality regarding the arbitrary resolution of problems in the municipality's territory by responsible persons and in order to establish the facts, "I hereby order: " Do you want me to read the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. On the basis of what you've read out just now, it seems that the basis for this order that was signed by General Pavkovic was the fact that they received anonymous information from citizens of the municipality of Istok about the problems that were present in the municipality. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what citizens. I know that this happened -- or, rather, I assumed this happened on the 12th of April when Mr. Pavkovic was in Istok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Pantic, can you please tell me when it is that you first saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen it before coming here to The Hague. Actually, when I talked to The Hague investigators in Belgrade, I asked them to show this to me but they didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we now please have -- rather, in paragraph 54 of your statement, you say -- or, rather, you refer to P1721. So could we please call this document up in e-court. My next question: When was it you first saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Also in The Hague when I came here three or four days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 54 as well, that is one, two, three -- the third subparagraph, the one-but-last sentence, you analyse this document and you say: "Had they talked to me I would have explained and such terms would not have been used." In relation to that, I would like to ask you whether you know who Major Blagoje Pesic is.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's not a major, he's a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sorry, captain. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether he was a member of the staff of the MUP during the war -- or, rather, in April 1999? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a member of the staff, but I do know that he was on the commission that was established then. Whether he was a member of the staff, I don't know, because my communication ended at the Pec secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that during the course of this interview with the investigators of the OTP you stated that on the 14th of April you made a statement -- or, rather, you talked to Blagoje Pesic about all these events and conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to 2006?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Did you state that then, that on the 14th of April, 1999, Captain Pesic talked to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I worked with Blagoje Pesic in 2002 and 2003 in the staff at Kursumlija when I learned that he was a member of the staff. That was in 2002 and 2003. And in 1999 I didn't know that, but since he's my neighbour, I knew that he was a commander of the police station in Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, perhaps we did not understand each other. My question was did you, in talking to the OTP representatives on the 22nd of March, 2006, did you tell them in relation to this commission and the arrival in Istok that Captain Blagoje Pesic personally talked to you on the 14th of April, 1999? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: He talked to me on the 14th of April, 1999, yes, that's true. But at the time I didn't know that he was a member of the staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's fine. And that wasn't the point of my question whether he was a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I gave a statement to him. Everybody else had left, and I remained there to give him a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 54, in the last sentence you say that you had never received this report, and you just mentioned when was the last time you saw it. Could we now once again see P1720 again on our screens. I'm interested in paragraph 3. Mr. Pantic, would you please read this sentence to us.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: You mean paragraph 3, item 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: "The commission will work from the 14th until the 15th of April, 1999, following which they are to -- to provide a written report to me and suggest measures concerning the situation established."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So the president of the commission had duty to inform General Pavkovic only about the facts?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. If the commission is established, then normally members of the commission should also take part in compiling the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a different matter. I told you this: In the last sentence in the paragraph that you read you said that this was never submitted to you, and my position is that the commission did not have the duty to provide a report about the situation to anyone else but the person who had issued this order originally?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Item 3 speaks about the time period during which the commission was supposed to work so the commission was established and they were to compile a report and inform Mr. Pavkovic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. Am I right in saying that when you had an interview with the OTP you stated that you were in charge of the town of Istok and that you did not go to any of the villages outside of Istok and that you have no direct knowledge about what was taking place, that you moved your family to Istok, and that only on two occasions unless I'm mistaken you went to a funeral, to a village that was outside of Istok, and that you also attended an on-site investigation due to NATO bombing in late January in the prison of Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Can we take it point by point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Whether I moved my family to -- outside of Istok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, to Istok.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Well, in the same building where we were when the bombing took place, we together with Albanians cleared the area, and then my family was moved to the basement of the same building where we lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you leave and, if so, how often the town of Istok?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Only if it was necessary to attend a meeting in Pec with the chief of secretariat or if there was any other need to go out in the field to tour some places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in just one more issue. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: You also asked this and I don't want to leave it unanswered, whether I attended any funerals outside of Istok, and I did when three members of the army were killed in the village of Lubazde [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to repeat my question because you were asked whether in the vicinity of the prison there was a forward command post of the army of Yugoslavia and you answered that question and you said that the first time you left town was when there was this funeral of the soldiers and the other time was on the 21st or 25th of February when the entire team conducted on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the prison there was no forward command post of the army. It was located in another municipality altogether, not in the municipality of Istok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, I represent General Lazarevic. I will have a couple of questions for you. And I will follow up on what Mr. Aleksic asked you which concerns the parts of your statement where you spoke about the order of the commander of the 69th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this: You spoke about this commission. You answered these questions of Mr. Aleksic. I'm interested in this: After military and territorial departments were resubordinated to the command of the Pristina Corps in the second part of April, do you know that the corps commander issued an order whereby he cancelled or stayed all decisions and disallowed the interference of units into the work of civilian authorities, Crisis Staffs, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the order, but I know when this 7th Infantry Brigade arrived, and there was also either a platoon or a company of military police under the command of Matic. When they arrived the situation was drastically changed. Things started working properly. We established cooperation with police. The military -- or, rather, the cooperation between police, the military, and the civilian authorities was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. The exhibit I was referring to was 5D374, Your Honours, and this is the order of the command of the Pristina Corps. It has already been admitted into evidence and shown here a number of times. I'm satisfied with this answer of Mr. Pantic. Mr. Pantic, in item 23 of your statement, rather, paragraph 23 of your statement you spoke about the killing of five soldiers. I would simply like to get more details, and therefore I'll ask you whether this pertains to the soldiers who worked in the signals units in the infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were in the signals units but I know that they were soldiers of the 7th Infantry Brigade and this happened on the road between Mitrovica and Pec near the place called Citak. They encountered a mine in their vehicle, and it was then that five members of the army of Yugoslavia were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantic. In paragraph 31 of your statement you spoke about the cooperation with the army of Yugoslavia and the military police, and in the last sentence you said: "Sometimes we were unable to do this because members of the army refused to provide even basic particulars to us." Who did you have in mind when you said "members of the army"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Those were people wearing camouflage uniforms. Perhaps we were unable to establish their identity. Perhaps they were civilians wearing camouflage uniforms, because at that time people were selling uniforms to hunters, similar looking uniforms to hunters, and what we had, we wrote down what their appearance was and we gave it to the army to establish their identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you were referring to people whom you noticed out there in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: Yes, whom we noticed and we apprehended as perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantic. In paragraph 34 you spoke -- or, rather, you provide an example which took place in the village of Zlokucane, Glina municipality. Do you know that officer Maric and this military unit belonged to 202nd logistics base and this is a quartermaster's unit, a noncombat unit who was headquartered there providing assistance to Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR PANTIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the brigade that they belonged to. I personally went there because I had a moral duty to visit some Albanians who were of Catholic religion because my family owed them a favour back from 1941. So I took medicine and food to them.
